scenarios:
A graduate student working on a thesis needs to collect, cite, and organize millions of research papers; they use the tool to add PDFs as Markdown notes with justifications, automatically build a knowledge graph of related concepts, and pull up the most relevant single-page summary for each research question.  

A data‑science team is preparing a weekly sprint report; they record every experiment as a note, tag it by the associated project, and use the bounded RAG lookup to quickly surface all dependencies and downstream tasks for a sprint meeting.  

A product manager mapping out a new feature wants a visual overview of upcoming stories; they create a todo template for each feature, use the graph view to see parent/child stories, and export a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that is then inserted into the project’s Kanban board.  

An AI developer is debugging a complex inference pipeline; they add the pipeline’s logs as notes, query the local index by type “problem” to find related failures, and retrieve features that depend on a specific module to isolate the issue.  

A journalist researching a story creates a note for each source, learns the topic with cited references, and then uses the query_local functionality to pull a concise deck of the top three related investigations, making a quick briefing sheet for co‑hosts.  

An event planner documents venue arrangements, guests, and vendor contracts; the planner creates a checklist template for each event, queries related notes by tag, and exports a workflow diagram so staff can see the required hand‑offs between teams.

scenarios: When I’m an on‑call senior engineer stepping into a legacy codebase, I pull the repo into the system to get an instant project brief with key modules, risk levels, and next‑step recommendations—so I can orient myself without sifting through pages of code.

As a security analyst overseeing a recent merge, I let the tool inventory the changes, apply gated‑operation policies, and retrieve RAG takeaways that flag policy violations, giving me a quick safety check before the merge is approved.

While a product manager is drafting a sprint plan, I use the code‑map view to see how components interconnect and which parts can be safely delegated or postponed, helping to prioritize features with a clear visual map.

During a compliance audit, I ask the system to scan read‑only snapshots of all repos, generate cited project briefs, and confirm adherence to all registry policies—providing the auditors with audit‑ready documentation.

When my team is tidying logic from a monolith toward micro‑services, the tool gives me a bounded priority set of services, stores their RAG takeaways, and keeps the source repo untouched, so we can schedule work confidently.

When onboarding a new developer, I hand them the system’s generated project brief, the key actives, and the OpenClaw continuity worker that can immediately surface the next tasks on their queue, speeding up their ramp‑up.
